definition: Dlib is a general purpose cross-platform software library written in the programming language C++.
details: Its design is heavily influenced by ideas from design by contract and component-based software engineering. Thus it is, first and foremost, a set of independent software components. It is open-source software released under a Boost Software License. Since development began in 2002, Dlib has grown to include a wide variety of tools. As of 2016, it contains software components for dealing with networking, threads, graphical user interfaces, data structures, linear algebra, machine learning, image processing, data mining, XML and text parsing, numerical optimization, Bayesian networks, and many other tasks. In recent years, much of the development has been focused on creating a broad set of statistical machine learning tools and in 2009 Dlib was published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research. Since then it has been used in a wide range of domains.

explainer.lead: Dlib is an open-source C++ toolbox for building software across many platforms. It combines general programming components with a broad set of statistical machine-learning tools, so developers can use it for much more than machine learning alone.

tiers.eli5: Dlib is like a big toolbox for people writing computer programs in C++. Instead of making every tool themselves, programmers can pick ready-made pieces for jobs such as learning from data, working with pictures, or doing calculations. The pieces are designed to work independently, so you can take only the ones you need.
tiers.practitioner: Use Dlib as a collection of independent C++ components rather than as a single machine-learning framework. Its machine-learning, linear-algebra, numerical-optimization, and image-processing components can support statistical learning work, while networking, threading, GUI, and parsing components cover surrounding application needs. Its contract-oriented, component-based design and broad scope are worth keeping in mind when choosing which parts to adopt.
tiers.paperLevel: Dlib is an open-source, cross-platform C++ component library whose design draws on design by contract and component-based software engineering. A 2009 Journal of Machine Learning Research publication documented Dlib, whose development has increasingly emphasized statistical machine learning alongside numerical optimization, linear algebra, Bayesian networks, and image processing.

explainer.example: A small image-analysis program could use Dlib's image-processing components to handle pictures, its linear-algebra and numerical-optimization components for calculations, and its statistical machine-learning tools for the learning part. If the program also needs a graphical interface, it can use Dlib's GUI components as well.

explainer.intuition: Think of Dlib as a set of well-defined building blocks: each component handles a particular job, and a program combines only the blocks it needs.
howItWorks: A developer writes a C++ application for a supported platform.
The application selects independent Dlib components for the required tasks.
Contracts and component-based design guide how those pieces are used.
Machine-learning components can be combined with linear algebra, optimization, image processing, and other utilities.
explainer.whyItMatters: Dlib brings general application utilities and statistical machine-learning tools into one cross-platform C++ library. Its independent components let developers adopt relevant functionality without treating the whole library as a single machine-learning system.
misconceptions: Dlib is not only a machine-learning library; its components cover many other programming tasks.
Dlib is not a single model or algorithm, but a collection of software components.
Its components are designed to be independent rather than one fixed processing pipeline.
